text:
Open the experiment’s envelope
Write down your measured motion, radius ratio and event midpoint before running the next cell. Injection truth now becomes available for comparison. It was not used by the measurement pipeline. A controlled experiment can expose a biased answer even when its plots look convincing.
Compare like quantities. Geometric depth k² is a ratio of projected areas; maximum dimming of a limb-darkened star is different. The designed area ratio is about 1.343%; peak dimming additionally depends on the adopted intensity law, trajectory and exposure integration. The motion target is about 94.8 mas/year across ten simulated years. Compare deviations with the stated errors rather than rounding them away.


Science Explanation

Existing qualification repeated the pipeline with five independent exposure- noise seeds on this fixed scene. All motion, radius-ratio and timing recoveries fell within three reported errors. Five draws give only a rough check, not a precise estimate of statistical coverage across arbitrary fields. They do not sample different stellar populations or uncertain orbital, spectrum, limb-darkening and instrument parameters. The underlying analytic field has no coadd-measurement error; this simplification is part of the qualification boundary. These historical checks describe this Model Sky configuration; results from other scenes are not substituted for them.
Negative controls ask whether the procedure reports a signal when it should not: stationary targets, constant light, deliberately incompatible reference coordinates and fully masked inputs. The contaminated cadence should be rejected. An intentionally wrong PSF tests model sensitivity; earlier qualification found biased flux and worse residuals. These are historical tests with their own package receipts, not additional experiments silently performed by this truth-display cell. Fresh execution establishes that this notebook runs; it does not expand those scientific coverage claims.

Extension · Shorten the baseline, keep the star
The optional cell rebuilds a separate controlled bundle with two years of motion instead of ten. It reuses the Model Sky analytic calibration and physical configuration, preserves the shared inputs, and writes a separate bundle under results/. Predict whether the dipole still determines a unique displacement. A shorter interval makes the lobes overlap more closely.
Run once in a fresh output directory. A message that motion is unconstrained is informative for this case; it is not an instruction to relax the guard until the intended answer appears.


Science Explanation

For a small shift vector Δ, a difference between nearly overlapping PSFs is approximately proportional to source flux times Δ times the PSF gradient. A brighter source moving less can resemble a fainter source moving more. This is an identifiability problem: the data constrain a combination of parameters more strongly than each parameter alone.
The example rejects a fit when the absolute flux/separation correlation exceeds 0.98. That conservative guard is not a universal telescope resolution limit. A longer baseline or direct position fits in separate epochs can supply different information. Even with a fixed position error, converting to motion divides by elapsed time, so a shorter baseline increases the error in mas/year.


# Attendee opt-in; the executed reference enables this block.
RUN_BASELINE_EXERCISE = True
if RUN_BASELINE_EXERCISE:
    from dataclasses import replace
    from model_sky import SceneConfig, prepare_bundle
    # Separate generated dataset; refuse to overwrite an earlier experiment.
    variant_dir = OUTPUT / "baseline-2yr"
    if variant_dir.exists():
        raise FileExistsError("Choose a new output for this experiment")
    config = replace(SceneConfig(), baseline_years=2.0)
    prepare_bundle(root / manifest["calibration_dir"], variant_dir,
                   config=config)
    variant_root, variant_manifest = pipeline.load_bundle(variant_dir)
    variant_files = variant_manifest["files"]
    earlier = pipeline.read_exposure(pipeline.bundle_path(
        variant_root, variant_files["reference_old"]))
    later = pipeline.read_exposure(pipeline.bundle_path(
        variant_root, variant_files["motion"]))
    try:
        # Rejection can be correct when flux and separation are degenerate.
        recovered = pipeline.measure_motion(
            earlier, later, variant_manifest["target_search"]["old_xy"])
    except RuntimeError as exc:
        print("Motion is unconstrained for this experiment:", exc)
    else:
        factor = 1000 * variant_manifest["pixel_scale_arcsec"] / 2
        print("Two-year motion [mas/year]:",
              recovered["separation_pixels"] * factor,
              "+/-", recovered["separation_error_pixels"] * factor)

Motion is unconstrained for this experiment: overlapping dipole lobes trade flux against separation; use a longer baseline or direct epoch astrometry


For the prepared two-year case, the flux/separation guard reports that the motion is unconstrained. That outcome is part of the experiment: reducing the baseline removes information even though the same GPU fitting routine still runs. Preserve the rejection alongside the ten-year result instead of reporting the unstable fit as a second precise measurement.

section: Optional investigation · Could another system make this dip?
text:
Optional investigation · Could another system make this dip?
A dip alone does not establish a planet. An unresolved blend combines light from multiple sources in the same footprint. Two stars eclipsing each other can lose a great deal of their own light; a brighter neighbor dilutes that loss into a shallow dip that resembles a planetary transit.
The optional paired experiment uses the same Model Sky calibration and physical star model to compare a planet on the target with a fading neighbor. The nearby contaminant is added for this experiment; it is not an observed companion or a catalog entry. Each case supplies out-of-event and in-event images, independent 16-exposure averages at those light levels rather than complete time series. xFit fits centers of the source light profiles, a model-based centroid measurement, and locates the negative difference signal. A similar aperture depth can hide a different location for missing light. An aperture is a region whose pixels are summed.
Inspect the cyan reference-position marker and measured fading-light position. These controlled snapshots demonstrate source localization. They cannot reveal alternating eclipse depths or a second eclipse that was never observed, and a small offset does not prove a planet. Repeated events, additional colors, spectra and longer time coverage provide different tests.


Science Explanation

Here D = Iin − Iout, so the fitted fading source has negative amplitude. Aperture depth is 1 − Fin/Fout. Extra constant neighbor light contributes to both sums and reduces fractional depth. The difference image can instead locate the changing light.
Formal centroid errors condition on a chosen Gaussian model and estimated sky. The difference-source and reference centroid share pixels, so their separation has no independent significance claim. This does not propagate every PSF or background-model uncertainty. Bryson et al. (2013) describe centroid vetting for Kepler false positives.
Transit photometry measures light loss. Other planet searches measure different effects: radial velocity detects a star’s motion toward and away from us; astrometry detects its wobble across the sky; microlensing detects gravitational magnification; direct imaging separates companion light. Combining a mass constraint with radius can constrain density. See NASA’s detection-method overview and AAVSO follow-up photometry.


# Independent in/out snapshots locate missing light in two cases.
RUN_BLEND_EXTENSION = True
if RUN_BLEND_EXTENSION:
    import blend
    from model_sky import SceneConfig
    blend_result = blend.run(root, OUTPUT / "blend", config=SceneConfig(), sources=Path("sources.md"))
    show_dark(blend_result["layout"])
    print("Saved blend diagnostics to", blend_result["html"])


  





Saved blend diagnostics to results/blend/planet-or-blend.html


Compare the location of missing light with the target’s reference position. Similar total dimming can have different spatial explanations. These paired images support a localization lesson; they do not establish a planet or supply an independent significance for every centroid offset.
xScan is omitted from Model Sky. No trained model, classifier performance or inference is claimed for these images.

text:
Further reading
The bundled source list records scientific techniques, data attribution and model inputs. The text and glossary explain terms locally; these links support deeper reading when you have a network connection. Opening external references is optional for running or viewing the example.

display(Markdown(Path("sources.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")))




Sources and model assumptions · Model Sky
All astronomical arrays and instrument inputs are generated by model_sky.py and scene.py. No observational pixels, catalogs, coordinate solutions, measured PSFs, masks, calibration, filter curves or trained models are inputs. The modeled arrays and example code are provided under Apache-2.0. The four overview SVGs in assets/ are original teaching schematics.
The sky is a fixed noiseless field of fictional stars. Each exposure receives independent source Poisson and Gaussian sky/read noise, after seeing, dither and transparency. Pixels use nJy; variance uses nJy². The 4 m telescope, 560–700 nm top-hat band at 40% total efficiency, 0.2 arcsec/pixel, 20.5 AB mag/arcsec² sky and 5 electron read noise are explicit models. None describes an actual instrument. A 3100 K Planck spectrum sets the brightness at 146.42 pc for radius 0.2162 solar. It omits M-dwarf molecular absorption and extinction. The illustrative quadratic limb-darkening law (0.6, 0.15) is independently declared; it is not derived from uniform blackbody emission. The orbit is circular and the geometry fixed during radius/time fitting.

Charbonneau et al. (2009), GJ 1214 discovery inspires the story; our simulated star is at a different distance.
Updated GJ 1214 parameters inform the stellar radius and illustrative orbital geometry.
Mandel & Agol (2002) and Kreidberg (2015), batman describe physical limb-darkened transit models. We integrate over each 30 second exposure.
Alard & Lupton (1998) provides the image-subtraction context. Actual cuPhoton xRep, xPois and xFit GPU calls reproject planes, fit kernels and measure stars in this example.
Tyson et al. (2020) discusses real satellite trails; ours is a separately modeled teaching approximation.
Bryson et al. (2013) explains centroid vetting; a displaced source can explain a dip. A transit-like candidate still needs repeated events, spectra and other follow-up for confirmation.
AAVSO exoplanet photometry connects calibrated light curves to follow-up work.
cuPhoton documentation describes the product interfaces. xScan is explicitly omitted here; no classifier weights, scores or training stamps are included.
Bokeh standalone documents explain embedded offline interactions. Inspecting a view does not rerun fits.

Truth is stored separately and revealed only after measurement. Five noise realizations test conditional uncertainties, not all astrophysical systematics. Incorrect PSFs and limb-darkening changes probe model sensitivity; they do not fully marginalize over real atmosphere or instrument uncertainty.
title: Model Sky

text:
Science glossary
Dotted terms show a definition on hover or keyboard focus in the HTML. Click or tap one to jump to its entry here; your browser’s Back button returns to the reading position. In a notebook, the same links and native hover text work without an extension.


Adding errors in quadrature


Squaring independent uncertainty sizes, adding those squares, then taking the square root. This combines independent variance contributions; correlations require additional covariance terms.


Angular scale / pixel scale


How much angle on the sky corresponds to one image pixel. The model declares 0.20 arcseconds per pixel. Multiplying pixel separation by this scale gives an angle; converting that angle to a physical distance also requires the distance to the star.


Aperture / annulus


For photometry, an aperture is a selected region around a source; an annulus is a surrounding ring often used to estimate local sky. Aperture can also mean the telescope's light-collecting opening.


Arcsecond / milliarcsecond


An arcsecond is 1/3,600 of a degree, a unit of angle. A milliarcsecond (mas) is 1/1,000 of an arcsecond. mas/yr measures angular change per year; neither unit is a time interval despite the word second.


Astrometry


Measuring where objects appear on the sky and how those positions change. Image alignment and the moving star's position measurement are astrometric tasks.


Background / sky level


Light or detector signal surrounding the source being measured. A local sky estimate removes a nearby baseline level. The modeled background scene contains fixed fictional stars. Diffuse sky light contributes noise even though its mean level has been subtracted.


Bandpass / modeled band


The range of light wavelengths admitted by an instrument, weighted by its sensitivity. Model Sky uses a declared response from 560 to 700 nanometres. This interval is an idealized model, not a measured filter curve or a standard astronomical band.


Blackbody / Planck spectrum


An ideal thermal emitter whose smooth spectrum is set by its temperature through Planck's law. Here 3100 K, an assumed stellar radius and distance set the received light. Real cool stars have molecular absorption missing from this approximation; it is not a measured stellar spectrum.


Blend / unresolved source


Light from different objects overlaps too closely for the image to separate them. A faint eclipsing star behind the target can produce a dip attributed to the wrong object. Unresolved means the components are not separately distinguished.


Cadence


The timing or spacing of observations. Here one 30-second exposure starts each minute. A cadence can also mean one sample in that sequence; rejecting a cadence excludes that exposure from the measurement.


Calibration / calibrated flux


Putting measurements on a common physical or positional scale. Here the electron-to-nJy conversion, pixel scale and coordinate grid are declared model inputs. They keep units consistent within the experiment and do not represent calibration measurements from an actual camera.


Centroid


The estimated centre of an object's light distribution. Fitting several pixels can locate it to a fraction of a pixel. A changing centroid can reveal a blend or an alignment problem.


Check star


A separate star treated as steady and measured like the target, but kept out of the brightness correction. Its remaining fluctuations check whether quoted errors describe the scatter in this field.


Chi-square / reduced chi-square


A sum of squared data-minus-model differences divided by expected variances. Reduced chi-square divides by independent constraints left after fitting. Values above roughly one can signal underestimated errors or a poor model; correlations complicate that rule.


Coadd / averaged reference


An image combining aligned exposures, often by averaging. Each Model Sky reference is generated with the noise of a mean of 16 independent, equal-duration exposures. It still has noise shared by later measurements that reuse it. The underlying model sky itself is noiseless.


Comparison star / ensemble


A nearby star assumed steady during the sequence. Changes common to several such stars estimate changes in observing conditions. An ensemble combines their measurements to correct the target's light curve.


Conditional uncertainty


An error estimate holding stated assumptions fixed. Here the analytic sky, stellar properties, orbit and much of the detector model are fixed while exposure noise varies. Repeated noise realizations do not cover every way those model assumptions could be wrong.


Convolution


Replacing each pixel with a weighted combination of nearby pixels. The weights form a small array called a kernel. Here convolution broadens reference stars to match the science image's blur.


Correlated noise


Errors that move together. Resampling can reuse one input pixel in several output pixels, correlating their errors. A shared reference can also correlate measurements from different exposures.


Cosine / surface normal


Cosine describes the projection of one direction onto another: 1 when aligned and 0 at a right angle. A surface normal is perpendicular to a surface. In limb darkening, the angle describes how directly we view a patch of the star.


Covariance


A measure of how errors in two quantities vary together. A covariance matrix records these relationships as well as each quantity's variance. It matters when combining fitted positions into a separation error.


Degrees of freedom


Independent constraints remaining after fitting parameters. For a simple fit with independent errors, this is the number of data points minus the number of fitted parameters.


Difference image / difference flux


Science minus the PSF-matched reference and fitted background. Positive pixels mean extra light relative to that reference; negative pixels mean less. Difference flux measures the change, not all the light from a source.


Dipole


A paired positive and negative patch in a difference image. When a star moves, its new position leaves added light and its old position leaves missing light after subtraction. Dipole means two lobes here, not an electrical property of the star. Misaligned images can make similar patterns.


Direct imaging


Separating and detecting light from a planet beside its much brighter host star. This differs from inferring a planet through a change in the star's total light.


Displacement


A change in position with both size and direction. New position minus old position gives a two-component displacement in pixels. Its length is the separation.


Eccentricity


How stretched an orbit is: zero is a circle, while larger values below one describe increasingly elongated bound orbits. The adopted shape affects how fast a planet crosses the star.


Eclipse / eclipsing binary


Dimming when one body passes in front of another. An eclipsing binary is a pair of orbiting stars whose alignment causes dips. Its light can mimic a planet transit, especially when mixed with another star's light.


Electron / detector count


A particle carrying electric charge. A camera records charge produced when light is detected. Here electron counts are simulated using the declared telescope area, exposure time and efficiency, then converted to nJy. Photon-counting fluctuations and read noise enter in these count units; no raw camera counts are imported.


Empirical


Estimated from measurements rather than supplied as a model parameter. Here the measurement pipeline estimates PSFs from stars in the simulated images and error scales from their measured scatter. These estimates are independent of the withheld injection truth; empirical does not mean an observed astronomical image was imported.


Epoch


The time associated with an observation or reference position. The old and current motion epochs are simulated points ten years apart; the short transit sequence samples the current epoch.


Exoplanet


A planet outside our Solar System. A transit-shaped dip is evidence to investigate, not sufficient proof that an exoplanet caused it.


Exposure / visit


A period during which a detector collects light, and the resulting measurement. A visit is a telescope observation with timing and pointing. Each simulated exposure here averages incoming light over 30 seconds.


Exposure integration


Averaging the model over the time the detector collects light. A 30-second exposure does not measure a single instant; averaging can soften the transit's entry and exit compared with an instantaneous model.


Extinction


Dimming of starlight by absorption or scattering along its path, for example by interstellar dust. The Model Sky brightness calculation sets interstellar extinction to zero. That assumption is distinct from the instrument's modeled photon-detection efficiency.


False positive


A signal accepted as the event of interest even though another cause produced it. Blended eclipsing stars and instrumental changes can produce planet-like brightness dips.


FITS / HDU / plane


FITS is an astronomy file format for numerical arrays and metadata. Each header/data unit (HDU) is one named or numbered section. A plane here is a two-dimensional array: brightness, estimated variance, or pixel-quality flags on matching coordinates.


Flux / flux density


A measure of received light. This example uses nJy, a flux-density unit describing brightness per unit frequency. Summing or fitting a star's pixel pattern estimates its total brightness in that band.


Forced PSF photometry


Fitting a known star-shaped light pattern at a supplied position to measure brightness. Forced means the position is supplied even if that exposure alone has too little signal to detect the source.


Gaussian


A smooth bell-shaped function used to approximate blur or random-error distributions. A Gaussian-polynomial basis combines bell shapes with coordinate-dependent terms to describe more varied kernels.


Gradient / propagated error


A gradient records how a result changes for a small change in each input. Error propagation uses those sensitivities and the input covariance to estimate the result's uncertainty. This approximation is local to the fitted values.


Gravitational microlensing


Temporary brightening when a foreground object's gravity bends and magnifies light from a more distant star. A planet can alter that pattern, providing a detection method distinct from transits.


Ground truth / injection


Known values used to create a simulated signal, such as position or planet radius. An injection adds that controlled signal to the scene. Truth is withheld from measurement so recovery can be checked afterward.


Identifiability / degeneracy


Whether data can distinguish parameter choices. A brighter star with smaller motion can produce nearly the same pattern as a fainter star with larger motion; their values are then degenerate. A converged fit does not resolve this ambiguity by itself.


Image-matching kernel / basis


A small array of convolution weights reshaping the reference to match the science image. The basis supplies allowed patterns whose coefficients are fitted. This differs from a GPU program kernel or a notebook's Python process.


Impact parameter


How far from the star's apparent centre the planet passes at mid-transit, measured in stellar radii. Zero crosses the centre; a value near one passes near the edge and changes the shape and duration.


Interpolation / resampling


Estimating values between existing samples. Here, reprojection resamples input pixels onto a new grid using weighted neighbours. This changes how noise is shared between pixels; it does not create new independent data.


Latent sky / noiseless scene


The underlying expected image before random measurement noise is drawn. Here it is built from fictional stars and analytic light profiles. Each exposure applies its own blur, shift and brightness changes before receiving independent noise. Reusing this noiseless model does not reuse a previous exposure's random errors.


Least-squares fit


Choosing parameters to minimize squared data-minus-model differences. Weighting gives more reliable measurements more influence, often by dividing each squared difference by its estimated variance.


Light curve


Brightness plotted against time. Here each point is one exposure's brightness after correcting changes shared with comparison stars. A transit appears as a temporary downward dip.


Light-year


The distance light travels in one year in vacuum, about 9.46 trillion kilometres. It is a distance, not a duration.


Limb darkening


The star's visible edge is dimmer than its centre, so a crossing planet blocks different amounts of light along its path. This experiment declares a quadratic intensity law with coefficients 0.6 and 0.15. That shape is prescribed separately from the blackbody calculation of the star's total brightness.


Magnitude / AB magnitude


Astronomy's logarithmic brightness scale: smaller numbers mean brighter objects, and five magnitudes correspond to a factor of 100 in brightness. The AB convention uses a reference flux density of 3631 Jy. The modeled star has AB magnitude about 17.54 through the declared bandpass.


Marginal variance / uncertainty


Here marginal variance means one pixel's individual variance, a diagonal entry of the joint covariance. It does not include cross-pixel covariance or imply that kernel-fit uncertainty was integrated out. In other contexts marginalizing parameters means averaging over their possible values.


Mask


Flags or Boolean selections describing which measurements a stage may use. A quality mask records defects; a fit mask selects allowed pixels. Check the convention: True can mean included for a fit mask and excluded for a trail mask. Masking discards information.


Mid-transit time


The time at the centre of the transit. The fit estimates when the crossing is centred relative to the sequence's time origin. This differs from measuring the orbital period between repeated transits.


NaN / invalid measurement


A missing or invalid numerical result. A rejected exposure receives NaN flux rather than zero: zero would be a real brightness measurement and could falsely imply that the star disappeared.


nJy (nanojansky)


One nanojansky is 10⁻⁹ jansky, or 10⁻³⁵ watts per square metre per hertz. Here each pixel contains its contribution to modeled flux density. Summing or fitting a star's pattern estimates its brightness in the declared band. Variance in nJy² describes squared brightness uncertainty.


Noise / photon noise


Random variation in a measurement. Photon arrivals fluctuate even for a steady star; sky light and the detector add variation too. Reusing one noisy image copies its errors instead of generating independent exposures.


Normalization / relative flux


Rescaling to a chosen reference. A normalized PSF has pixel weights adding to 1. A light curve divided by its usual brightness is near 1; 0.99 is one per cent dimmer. Comparison-star normalization corrects changes shared across the field.


Orbit / orbital period


The path of one body around another under gravity. The orbital period is the time for a full circuit. The example assumes a period from its chosen model; one short transit sequence does not measure it.


Orbital inclination


The tilt of the orbit relative to the sky plane. In the transit model, 90 degrees means the orbit is viewed edge-on, making a crossing possible.


Parallax


An apparent position shift caused by a changing viewpoint. Annual parallax follows Earth's orbit and helps measure distance. This experiment models a star's linear proper motion only; it includes no annual parallax signal and does not measure the assumed stellar distance.


Parsec (pc)


A distance unit of about 3.26 light-years. One parsec corresponds to a star with annual parallax of one arcsecond. The simulated star's 146.42 pc distance is an assumption, not a distance measured here.


Photometry


Measuring an object's brightness. This notebook fits the star's expected pattern to pixels and repeats the measurement through time to obtain a light curve.


Photon


A quantum, or discrete packet, of light. A detector converts incoming photons into an electrical signal. Photon arrival counts fluctuate, so even a perfectly steady source has measurement noise.


Poisson statistics


A model for independent random event counts. For a mean count N, count variance is N and standard deviation is √N. Calibrated flux units and detector/background effects must be included before applying this rule to image values.


Positive / negative lobe


One patch of a dipole's two-part pattern. The positive lobe has more light in science than reference; the negative lobe has less. Negative values describe subtraction, not physically negative light.


Proper motion


A star's gradual angular movement across the sky, usually in milliarcseconds per year. It is not the full three-dimensional speed; converting to a sideways physical speed also requires distance.


PSF (point-spread function)


The pixel pattern made by one unresolved point of light. Preparation uses a Gaussian profile plus each exposure's common seeing blur for both field and target stars. Measurement estimates a PSF from image stars without reading that input profile. Matching PSFs makes images comparable before subtraction.


Radial velocity


Speed toward or away from the observer. A planet and star orbit their common centre of mass; changes in the star's radial velocity can reveal the planet. This needs spectral observations, not just the transit light curve.


Radius ratio / transit depth


Radius ratio k is planet radius divided by star radius. For a small planet crossing a uniformly bright star, fractional blocked light is about k². Limb darkening and the crossing path change the actual dip. Physical planet radius also needs an assumed stellar radius.


Read noise


Random variation introduced when detector electronics read accumulated charge. It can occur even with no incoming light. The model assigns 5 electrons of standard deviation per pixel per exposure and combines its variance with sky noise before converting to nJy².


Reference / template


The comparison image against which science is measured. An old-position reference reveals motion. A current-position, outside-transit reference measures dimming at the present location. The reference also has noise.


Registration


Aligning images so the same array coordinates describe the same sky position. WCS metadata gives the initial mapping; stationary neighbouring stars check the remaining alignment error.


Residual


What remains after subtracting a model from data. In image subtraction it highlights changes and mismatches. After a dipole or transit fit, structured leftovers can show that the model missed something.


RMS (root mean square)


Square each value, average the squares, then take the square root. For residuals this summarizes typical size in original units without positive and negative values cancelling. Large outliers strongly affect it.


Sampling / undersampling


Representing a continuous pattern with finite pixels or time steps. Undersampling means too few samples to resolve its shape. Subpixel describes positions or model steps finer than one detector pixel; it does not add new observed pixels.


Saturation


A detector or recorded value reaching its usable upper limit. Such a pixel no longer reliably measures how much light arrived. Model Sky does not simulate saturation; real-camera data would need suitable quality flags and detector-specific limits.


Science image


The exposure being investigated, compared with a reference image. Registered science is that measurement resampled onto the reference grid. Science here labels the image's role in the comparison.


Seeing


Blurring and distortion caused by Earth's turbulent atmosphere. Here a declared blur varies across exposures and affects all stars in each exposure consistently. It illustrates changing image quality without importing an atmospheric measurement or simulating all turbulence effects.


Signal-to-noise ratio (S/N)


Signal size compared with estimated random uncertainty. Higher values make random fluctuations a less plausible explanation, but do not rule out systematic errors or a wrong model.


Sky plane / line of sight


The sky plane describes directions across the image, perpendicular to the direction toward the observer. Motion in this plane changes apparent position; line-of-sight motion is toward or away from us.


Spectrum / stellar atmosphere


A spectrum describes light at each wavelength or frequency. A stellar atmosphere is the outer gas that shapes a star's escaping light. Model Sky uses a smooth blackbody spectrum in place of an atmosphere model; molecular absorption and other spectral features are omitted.


Stamp


A small image cutout around an object or candidate. Fitting a stamp uses nearby pixels without processing the full field for each source.


Standard deviation / sigma


A measure of spread, equal to the square root of variance. For an accurate Gaussian error model about 68% of repeated errors fall within ±1 sigma. That interpretation needs the model assumptions to hold.


Stellar radius / solar radius


The distance from a star's centre to its visible surface. A solar radius uses the Sun's radius as a unit. Here an assumed stellar radius turns the fitted planet-to-star radius ratio into a planet size.


Sum / summation


Adding a collection of numbers. The symbol Σ means sum over the stated index. A weighted sum first multiplies each value by its weight; a weighted average divides by the total weight.


Systematic errors / systematics


Repeatable biases or patterns left by calibration, observing conditions or a wrong model. More samples may not average them away. Comparison stars and residuals help expose some of them.


Throughput / instrument response


The fraction of incoming light converted into recorded signal after all optical and detector losses. Here the declared total photon efficiency is 0.4 from 560 to 700 nanometres and zero outside that band. This is an optical model input, not GPU operations per second.


Time baseline


Elapsed time between position measurements. A longer interval lets a slowly moving star travel farther in the image. The default ten-year interval is an input to the simulated motion experiment; it is not elapsed observing time or the length of the short transit sequence.


Top-hat response


An idealized response that is constant inside a specified interval and zero outside it, with sharp edges. The Model Sky passband has this shape from 560 to 700 nanometres. Real filters generally have rounded edges and wavelength-dependent sensitivity.


Transit / ingress / egress


A planet or other body crossing in front of its star as seen by us, temporarily blocking starlight. Ingress is entry onto the visible disc; egress is exit. The example creates a simulated planet transit with a physical light-curve model.


Uncertainty / formal error


An estimate of precision under stated assumptions. Formal fit error comes from the fit model and supplied noise. It can omit alignment errors, shared-reference errors or wrong assumptions; it is not a guaranteed bound.


Uncertainty coverage


For uncertainty checks, the fraction of repeated experiments whose error interval contains the true value. A few successful trials cannot establish that fraction precisely. Image coverage means which sky area or pixels are available.


Variance


Expected squared fluctuation around a mean. Its square root is the standard deviation. Brightness in nJy has variance in nJy². A per-pixel variance plane records individual error sizes but not all correlations between pixels.


Wavelength / frequency


Wavelength is the spacing between successive crests of a light wave. Frequency counts its oscillations per second. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength; visible colours correspond to different wavelengths.


WCS (World Coordinate System)


Metadata mapping pixels to sky coordinates. Right ascension and declination locate a direction, like longitude and latitude on Earth. Here the grid and exposure shifts are declared inputs around RA 210 degrees and Dec −10 degrees, not a solution fitted to a catalog. Stationary stars still check the image-registration accuracy.


Reprojection


Resampling an image onto a specified sky coordinate grid using a supplied coordinate mapping. It does not itself estimate alignment corrections from stars.


These definitions describe the Model Sky experiment. See the NASA FITS primer, Astropy WCS documentation, Astropy blackbody model, NASA planet-detection overview and the primary papers linked beside each Science Explanation.
title: Model Sky

text:
17.1 A scene, a detector, and a unit
GPU reference run from cuPhoton d0d4497a.
This notebook exercises xImage (cuphoton.ximage), cuPhoton’s component for reconstructing a common static scene from registered exposures. We also use its separate PSF-calibration workflow to estimate the blur of each exposure.
Model Scene starts with generated, already registered arrays, supplied noise variances and per-exposure PSFs. The FITS-reading and registration boxes show where xImage fits in a broader workflow. A reconstructed scene could become a reference for subtraction, but its effective PSF and output uncertainty need qualification before use with xPois. See the component architecture for the data contracts between stages.
These three examples use independently modeled inputs and can be read separately:
A sharp-looking image can give a biased measurement. Here we reconstruct one static modeled field from eight blurred exposures and ask whether the result predicts four exposures that the solver never saw. We measure flux against independent modeled truth, then deliberately break the PSF, noise and static-scene assumptions. Every pixel comes from the analytic models distributed with this example. No astronomical imagery, survey calibration, or downloaded catalog is used.
Notebook source on GitHub
The full reference contains at least 50 independent noise realizations, with identical draws shared between methods. A quick run exercises the APIs and plots; its small sample supports no performance conclusion. All HTML selectors choose saved results. They do not rerun a solver.
The latent scene contains two isolated stars, a close pair, and two extended Gaussian galaxies. Each source has a declared integrated flux, position and intrinsic width. A uniform background contributes two electrons per pixel per unit exposure. The stars have a small finite width of 0.22 pixel; their fine structure is deliberately undersampled.
matters when light changes appreciably within a pixel. Our physical renderer integrates continuous Gaussians over square pixels using normal-distribution CDF differences. Coordinates name pixel centers, and pixel edges lie half a pixel away. Flux units are electrons per unit exposure. Variance has the square of those units. All principal exposures have duration one, so counts and rates have the same numeric values.
The fixed catalog samples one on-grid pixel phase. Noise repetitions do not qualify other subpixel phases or a general source population.

text:
Pixel integration




Science Explanation: Continuous truth and discrete inference

For a Gaussian source of intrinsic width ss blurred by a Gaussian PSF of width pp, the continuous width is s2+p2\sqrt{s^2+p^2}. The integral of a unit one-dimensional Gaussian over pixel jj is
Pj=Φ((j+1/2−μ)/σ)−Φ((j−1/2−μ)/σ).P_j=\Phi((j+1/2-\mu)/\sigma)-\Phi((j-1/2-\mu)/\sigma).
The two-dimensional integral is the product of the two axis integrals. Source flux multiplies this unit integral. Finite-stamp losses remain visible; we do not renormalize each source into the image. The renderer uses no xImage convolution, torch operation or PSF helper. This independence exposes model representation errors that a shared generator and solver could conceal.
title: 17  Model Scene

text:
17.2 What an exposure measures

Point spread function (PSF)

describes how source light spreads across neighboring pixels. Twelve exposures have widths from 0.9 to 1.7 pixels and independent noise. They share a zero-dither grid. This experiment tests neither WCS alignment nor resampling.
In the main case, Gaussian noise has exactly known variance four. The physical generator performs continuous convolution before pixel integration. xImage applies finite, sampled kernels to a discrete latent image. Those operators differ slightly, especially for undersampled stars. The matched-operator control isolates that discrepancy by generating observations with a separate SciPy discrete convolution.


Science Explanation: The forward model

For exposure ee and pixel ii, the inference model is
yei=(Hex)i+nei,nei∼𝒩(0,vei).y_{ei}=(H_e x)_i+n_{ei},\qquad n_{ei}\sim\mathcal N(0,v_{ei}).
Here xx includes the known constant background, HeH_e denotes the supplied fixed PSF convolution, and the independent variances veiv_{ei} are positive. A symmetric Gaussian PSF simplifies the teaching field; separate asymmetric operator controls are needed to detect a kernel flip or transpose. Four held-out frames test a different blur of the same scene. Their noise is independent, although their prediction uncertainty comes from the fitted image.
title: 17  Model Scene

section: 17.3 Read the array contract before fitting
text:
17.3 Read the array contract before fitting
Images, variances, masks and background use (batch, y, x, frame). PSFs use (kernel_y, kernel_x, channel, frame). The singleton batch and channel axes have different meanings. A transpose that preserves array rank can still change the science.
Masks are boolean: True means good. The outlier generator records which pixels it contaminated, and the explicit-mask investigation uses that record. This is an idealized quality flag, not a claim that a detector would identify all outliers. The example rejects nonfinite or nonpositive variances before starting a fit. Exposure normalization divides intensity by time and variance by time squared, exactly once. Counts-versus-rates controls exercise the actual workflow preprocessing.


Code
from cuphoton.ximage.data import load_ximage_bundle, validate_bundle
with load_ximage_bundle(STUDY / "trial-000/l2-bundle") as bundle:
    print("Bundle validation:", validate_bundle(bundle))
    print("Images:", bundle.images.shape, "PSFs:", bundle.psfs.shape)
    print("Good-mask dtype:", bundle.masks.dtype)
    assert np.all(np.isfinite(bundle.variances))
    assert np.all(bundle.variances > 0)

title: 17  Model Scene

text:
17.4 Build the ordinary coadd

Coadd

reduces independent noise. It also mixes the exposure PSFs. Averaging eight images does not by itself establish finer spatial resolution. Equal Gaussian variances make equal weights appropriate for this experiment. The image-level comparison first blurs each constituent to a common attainable Gaussian width of 2.4 pixels, then averages. Reconstruction receives the corresponding additional blur. This comparison spends resolution to make flux measurements comparable. Discrete smoothing approximates continuous blur, and the noiseless physical control measures the residual bias floor.


Science Explanation: Why the target resolution is broader

A Gaussian blur adds variances. To turn a width pep_e exposure into a width qq target, the additional blur has width q2−pe2\sqrt{q^2-p_e^2}, which requires q≥peq\ge p_e. We choose q=2.4q=2.4 before evaluating the test scene. A coadd PSF is a mixture of the exposure PSFs; it generally has no single Gaussian width. Blurring each constituent separately avoids replacing that mixture with an unjustified single Gaussian. The source’s intrinsic width remains part of the target image.
title: 17  Model Scene

text:
17.5 Reconstruct with xImage L2

Reconstruction

uses eight frames and fixed kernels. It solves no PSF parameters. The visible call below repeats the first saved fit with the same recorded configuration. The full study performs paired L2 and Huber fits on each noise realization.


Science Explanation: The weighted objective

The L2 objective is proportional to
L(x)=12∑e,imei[yei−(Hex)i]2vei,x≥0.L(x)=\frac12\sum_{e,i}m_{ei}\frac{[y_{ei}-(H_ex)_i]^2}{v_{ei}},\qquad x\ge0.
The mask mm is one for valid pixels. Pixels with larger variance receive less weight. Multiplicative updates preserve nonnegativity under their supported positive-kernel assumptions. An update stopping score is not a confidence interval. Iteration count regularizes this finite inverse problem; the reference fixes 300 iterations, a constant Huber threshold, and a very small stopping tolerance after a separate development-scene iteration sweep. The Huber threshold of two was declared in advance and was not tuned by that sweep.



Code
import yaml
from cuphoton.ximage.workflows import run_reconstruction
config = yaml.safe_load((STUDY / "trial-000/l2.yaml").read_text())
config["output"]["name"] = "notebook-l2"
config_path = ROOT / "notebook-l2.yaml"
config_path.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(config))
l2_run = run_reconstruction(config_path)
print(l2_run.summary["trace_summary"])
huber_config = yaml.safe_load((STUDY / "trial-000/huber.yaml").read_text())
huber_config["output"]["name"] = "notebook-huber"
huber_path = ROOT / "notebook-huber.yaml"
huber_path.write_text(yaml.safe_dump(huber_config))
huber_run = run_reconstruction(huber_path)
print(huber_run.summary["trace_summary"])

text:
17.6 Compare robust losses

Huber loss

limits the influence of large standardized residuals. It can help when a small fraction of pixels have large positive artifacts. Robustness also changes the response to ordinary noise and model mismatch. It need not improve every source or metric. Our threshold is two standardized residual units throughout the fit. A changing threshold would make the loss trace a sequence of different objectives.


Science Explanation: Residual scale and weighting

For r=(y−Hx)/vr=(y-Hx)/\sqrt v, the Huber loss is
ρδ(r)={r2/2,|r|≤δ,δ(|r|−δ/2),|r|>δ.\rho_\delta(r)=\begin{cases}r^2/2,&|r|\le\delta,\\
\delta(|r|-\delta/2),&|r|>\delta.\end{cases}
Scaling all variances by four divides standardized residuals by two. It changes the effective Huber transition in the original intensity units. The numerical control compares this with doubling the threshold. L2’s exact minimizer is unchanged by a global variance factor, while its reported objective rescales. Finite arithmetic and weakly constrained halo pixels can break exact numeric invariance; the controls record that boundary sensitivity.

text:
17.7 Keep real border context
The 15×15 kernel acts on a 96×96 fitting region inside a 120×120 generated field. The saved reconstruction is 110×110 because VALID convolution retains a seven-pixel latent halo. Forward convolution produces 96×96 context predictions. The page and primary measurements use the central 48×48 science window, with pixel origin (36, 36) in the generated field. Kernels and noise are generated over the whole field; the science window has real surrounding measurements as well as latent kernel support.
The initial compact fitting experiment had enough support for convolution but insufficient separation from the poorly constrained latent boundary for the subsequent common-resolution blur. Some outer latent pixels grew very large and contaminated that blur. The compact experiment remains a deliberate boundary-failure control, and its original reference is retained separately. The revised context geometry was checked on development data before freezing fresh test seeds. Numerical records retain full-context prediction errors alongside the central-window errors, so the boundary limitation stays visible.
Apertures must lie at least five pixels from the science-window boundary. That exclusion defines the catalog measurement region; the larger fitting context supplies the additional support needed before blurring. Zero-valued padding never substitutes for a detector measurement in the fitting ROI.
The compact control shown here is a single draw and may have little source-aperture bias. In the preserved first 50-draw compact study, L2 mean errors at the two edge sources were +1.29% (SE 0.23%) and +0.66% (SE 0.16%). That failed study used its own split and seeds; these are historical failure evidence, not paired comparisons with revision 2. Its external reference-01/study/summary.json has SHA-256 27ae33705230110e6aafac7ea9112834b092702c966ae7c6cb5164cc4be5809c.

section: 17.8 Calibrate a PSF from independent star data
text:
17.8 Calibrate a PSF from independent star data

PSF calibration

has two distinct steps here. First, an example-authored estimator uses centered, zero-background calibration stars, clips negative noisy samples, and normalizes the stamp. Each idealized on-grid star supplies 100,000 electrons and independent Poisson photon counts plus Gaussian read noise. Its known centering avoids a shift-estimation problem. Second, run_psf_solve factors that measured stamp through a Gaussian reference. The public solver receives PSF images; it does not locate or fit stars.


Science Explanation: The Gaussian reference changes the target

PSF factorization approximates fe=g*hef_e=g*h_e, with reference width σg=0.55\sigma_g=0.55 pixel. Reconstructing with heh_e targets g*xg*x, rather than the unconvolved scene xx. The common-resolution comparison therefore adds only 2.42−0.552\sqrt{2.4^2-0.55^2} pixels of Gaussian blur to that product. Finite calibration noise, stamp clipping and imperfect factorization each contribute error. Perfect-known-kernel and independently repeated calibration draws separate those effects. A calibration error shared by several science realizations is a common systematic, not additional independent science noise.

The 0.55-pixel reference width is xImage’s package default and an explicit teaching choice in this protocol.

text:
17.9 Inspect the saved calibration kernels
Multiplicative PSF updates are the main investigation. Adam supplies an additional optimizer comparison. Adam can return negative kernel elements. The reference records its minimum, normalization and prediction error; such a kernel is excluded from multiplicative scene reconstruction when it violates positive-kernel assumptions. A small optimization loss alone does not establish a physically admissible calibrated kernel. The finite-calibration experiment repeats independent calibration draws on the same noiseless science scene. The plot reports noisy-calibration minus noiseless-calibration flux error, on the same noiseless science scene. Its scatter describes the chosen calibration model at the declared star flux. It does not establish survey calibration quality.

text:
17.11 Declare the flux endpoint

Aperture flux

is the primary endpoint: radius three pixels around each fixed catalog position, after matching resolution. We compare each aperture with the identical aperture on known target truth. These are local light measurements. They include neighbors and are not deblended total source fluxes. Fractional error is (measured − truth) / truth. We report every fixed source by input brightness and environment, plus class summaries. The catalog is small and fixed, so the experiment estimates noise sensitivity for these sources; it does not estimate a population-wide brightness or crowding law.


Science Explanation: Paired uncertainty and detectable bias

Each independent noise realization supplies one result per method. We form method differences within the same realization, preserving the covariance from shared input noise. We average sources within a class before estimating a class standard error across realizations. Sources in one image are not counted as independent noise realizations.
For NN independent trials, the estimated standard error of mean bias is s/Ns/\sqrt N. The page shows approximate 95% mean-bias intervals and reports 2.8s/N2.8s/\sqrt N as an approximate detectable bias at 80% power for a two-sided 5% test. Scatter estimates at N=50N=50 remain relatively imprecise. No broad method ranking follows from a difference smaller than its measured precision.

title: 17  Model Scene

text:
17.12 Positions, blends and extended light

Centroid

shifts when neighboring light enters an aperture. We compare measured centroids with target-truth aperture centroids. For the close pair we also record the distance between the two overlapping-aperture centroids and compare it with the intrinsic three-pixel separation. This deliberately simple estimator is biased by blending. A clean-looking pair cannot establish an unbiased deblended separation measurement. Annular mean-light profiles retain the extended-source evidence that a single sharpness number discards. The complete numerical artifacts include per-source profiles and centroid errors for every realization.
title: 17  Model Scene

section: 17.13 Predict exposures the solver never saw
text:
17.13 Predict exposures the solver never saw

Held-out prediction

tests whether one reconstructed scene explains different blurs. Select a frame below. Frames 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 11 were fitted; frames 3, 6, 10 and 12 were held out. This interleaves PSF widths rather than holding out only the broadest blurs. Residual means and spatial patterns matter alongside their magnitude. A residual second moment divided by known pixel variance is a diagnostic, not an automatic chi-square test with mean one. Fitting, positivity, spatial correlations and uncertainty in the predicted image change its interpretation. An independently noisy held-out frame removes one source of circularity, but it does not remove prediction uncertainty.

section: 17.14 Make the PSF wrong by five percent
text:
17.14 Make the PSF wrong by five percent
The next selector supplies kernels that are uniformly 5% too narrow or 5% too broad. Every exposure shares the sign of that error, including held-out kernels. A common PSF error can be absorbed partly into the inferred scene and evade a residual-only check. Truth-based aperture, centroid and profile errors quantify its measurement consequences. Small apertures and native-resolution profile fits can be more sensitive than common-resolution aperture flux. A weak flux effect is retained as a finite-sensitivity result. The coadd display uses the declared true widths for common-resolution smoothing in these controls. Its unchanged row is a known-model baseline, not a competing pipeline calibrated with the erroneous kernels.

section: 17.15 Separate outliers, variances and photon noise
text:
17.15 Separate outliers, variances and photon noise
The outlier case adds 100 electrons to roughly 0.3% of pixels. L2, Huber and an ideal explicit mask receive the same realization. Masking removes known contaminated measurements; Huber reduces influence according to residual size. They use different information, so the mask comparison is an idealized control.
Multiplying variances by four changes the interpretation of standardized residuals and Huber weighting. The photon/read-noise case instead draws Poisson electrons and adds Gaussian read noise. Its known variance equals expectation plus read variance. That likelihood differs from the exactly Gaussian principal case even though its first two moments are supplied. The page preserves the distinction when reporting results. The explicit quality mask applies to L2 and Huber reconstruction. The coadd remains the ordinary unmasked baseline in that control.
The photon/read example is one unpaired draw. It cannot resolve sub-percent bias.

17.16 Break the static-scene assumption

Transient

appears in a minority of frames at a new position in the central science window. A static fit can dilute its flux across the compromise image, redistribute light, or leave inconsistent frame residuals. The transient is present in fitted frames 2 and 7 and held-out frame 10. Select those frames and compare them with their neighbors. A robust loss may suppress variability that a time-domain analysis would want to preserve. This experiment has no classifier or alert stream; the evidence is the inconsistency of individual image predictions.

section: 17.17 What the native metrics can establish
text:
17.17 What the native metrics can establish
The native evaluator records coadd-relative PSNR, SSIM and sharpness. These diagnostics share input information and compare different effective resolutions. They describe image differences; they cannot establish reconstruction accuracy. The primary truth-based endpoint, independent calibration controls and individual held-out predictions supply the scientific qualification. The zero-dither experiment supports no claim about shift recovery, resampling covariance, WCS alignment or arbitrary super-resolution. The native evaluator uses its own median-coadd diagnostic reference. The primary comparison uses the separately constructed arithmetic coadd at the common target resolution.

text:
17.18 Reproduce and inspect the evidence
The execution receipt records source hashes, protocol hash, seeds, dependency versions and artifact hashes. The full numerical study stays outside Git. The page embeds selected first-realization arrays and complete summary diagnostics, keeping repeated-trial arrays out of the HTML. Every selector is a precomputed experiment selector. Reading the exported page requires no Python process, kernel, WebSocket, API, CDN or network connection.
See README.md for clean-environment execution and PUBLISHING.md for static packaging and the remaining versioned-Pages integration work. Opening or merging the source PR does not publish this chapter.
The reconstruction follows the ImageMM approach: Yashil Sukurdeep, Tamás Budavári, Andrew J. Connolly and Fausto Navarro, ImageMM: Joint Multi-frame Image Restoration and Super-resolution, The Astronomical Journal 170, 233 (2025). Cite that paper and the cuPhoton version printed by this execution. The declared teaching models and source catalog are original to this example.
title: 17  Model Scene

text:
The decision comes before the classifier
GPU reference run from cuPhoton d0d4497a.
A new image contains a bright spot. Is it a changing astronomical source, a detector defect, or the imperfect cancellation of a steady star? Model Alerts follows that decision from electrons in two exposures to the list a person reviews. We generate independent fields, detect positive changes with xPois, and train xScan from random initialization. xFit supplies an additional measured-feature investigation.
View the source notebook in NVIDIA/cuPhoton.
Every image, source, defect and noise realization is generated here from declared analytic models. No observed survey images or pretrained models enter the experiment. The results describe this modeled population. They do not establish survey performance or calibrated probabilities for the sky.
Read the expanded Science Explanations for assumptions, units and limitations. Follow a terminology link for a definition; keyboard focus and pointer hover also reveal it in the HTML. All plot controls explore saved arrays and scores in your browser. They do not train a new classifier.
We call a detected PSF-like appearance or brightening positive. Detector artifacts, noise peaks and residual light from static sources are negative. The first task is to define those words, before showing a model any labels.
An untrailed moving source is a genuine astrophysical challenge. We report it separately, rather than teaching the model that all motion is bogus. Overlapping changes and artifacts receive ambiguity flags. The complete candidate inventory retains them, while primary binary metrics state their coverage after excluding ambiguous associations and these challenges.

text:
Science Explanation

A label answers a scientific question about a detected candidate, not about an arbitrary image location. The distribution is conditional on passing the positive-detection rule. Pair classification therefore operates on subtraction-selected candidates even though its input omits the difference channel. Fading sources require a separate negative-polarity detection and labeling extension; positive-only recovery does not measure that task.
title: Model Alerts

section: Count electrons, then add independent noise
text:
Count electrons, then add independent noise
Our detector has unit gain: image values are electrons per pixel. A star has total expected flux FF electrons and a pixel-integrated circular Gaussian PSF. Reference seeing has σ=0.9\sigma=0.9–1.21.2 pixels; ordinary search seeing has σ=1.2\sigma=1.2–1.91.9 pixels. Background is uniform within an exposure and varies from 60 to 140 electrons per pixel. Read noise is 4 electrons RMS. These are teaching choices, not instrument measurements.


Science Explanation

For pixel pp, the expectation is

μp=b+∑jFj∫pP(x−xj,y−yj;σj)dxdy.\mu_p=b+\sum_j F_j\int_{p}P(x-x_j,y-y_j;\sigma_j)\,dx\,dy.

The PSF has units pixel−2^{-2} and integrates to one on the infinite plane. The generator integrates it over each pixel using error functions rather than sampling only the center. Exposures obey

Ip∼Poisson⁡(μp)+𝒩(0,σr2),Var⁡(Ip)=μp+σr2.I_p\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_p)+\mathcal N(0,\sigma_r^2),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(I_p)=\mu_p+\sigma_r^2.

The Poisson term is electron counting noise. Read noise is independent of it and of every other exposure. Finite image boundaries can truncate flux; injected source positions leave a declared margin. There is no saturation, clipping or masked-pixel generator signature. Registered detector-plane coordinates suffice here; no observed WCS or calibration product is used.

The declared artifact mixture has one persistent hot pixel (300–1500 expected electrons), one three-pixel cosmic ray (200–900 electrons per pixel), and one untrailed moving-source challenge (1800 expected electrons) per search epoch. Static stars span 400–18000 expected electrons. Registration combines a common 0.2-pixel Gaussian offset with independent 0.35-pixel offsets per star. Every seventh star has a 1.25× search PSF width. Brightening hosts are randomly chosen each epoch from the other stars, using the same PSF as their hosts. Shift-only column bleed spans 11 pixels with 100–400 added electrons per pixel; association uses distance to the full segment. These are teaching parameters, recorded in the design receipt.

design = Design()
y, x = np.indices((71, 71))
unit_psf = psf((71, 71), 34.2, 35.3, 1.5)
print("Integrated finite-field PSF flux:", unit_psf.sum())
print("Pixel centroid:", (unit_psf*x).sum(), (unit_psf*y).sum())
print("Declared generator:", design)

section: Independent fields own their repeated observations
text:
Independent fields own their repeated observations
The reference design starts with 300 fields and three search epochs per field: 180 training fields, 60 validation fields and 60 reserved test fields. Each field owns its stars, template noise, persistent defects and repeated epochs. The specified shift adds 60 independent fields. A development pilot runs before any reserved test field is generated.
The seed audit reads every generated development field, including fields with no detections, plus the CPU/CUDA agreement field. Reserved blocks and generator stream roles must be disjoint.


Science Explanation

Repeated exposures of one field share sky structure and a noisy template. Splitting their candidates independently would let the learner recognize the same structure on both sides of an evaluation boundary. We split fields first, then generate their observations from separate deterministic streams. Native provenance guards reject field identities crossing splits. We also audit seeds and duplicate candidate bytes. Different row IDs do not establish independence. If the primary validation field-bootstrap interval has half-width above five percentage points, we double the development design and reassess before freezing final counts and seed blocks.
title: Model Alerts

section: Create the residual that selects candidates
text:
Create the residual that selects candidates
xPois fits a Gaussian-polynomial convolution kernel and differential background from measured images. It does not use injected source locations as fitting masks. The residual is search minus the matched reference. We filter it with a fixed Gaussian of σ=1.4\sigma=1.4 pixels, then select local positive maxima above the development detection threshold. Cutouts are centered on those measured maxima.


Science Explanation

The image model and residual convention are

S≃R⊗K+B,D=S−(R⊗K+B).S\simeq R\otimes K+B,\qquad D=S-(R\otimes K+B).

Assumed unit gain, independent read-noise/background calibration and measured source intensity estimate input variances. For a fixed fitted kernel,

VD≃VS+VR⊗K2,q=D⊗HVD⊗H2.V_D\simeq V_S+V_R\otimes K^2,\quad
q=\frac{D\otimes H}{\sqrt{V_D\otimes H^2}}.

qq is a marginal detection diagnostic. It omits spatial covariance and kernel-fit uncertainty; it is not a calibrated Gaussian significance. The threshold is four in this diagnostic and the association radius is three pixels, both declared development choices and frozen before final testing. A complete stamp/kernel footprint is required. The same selection rule is used for pair, triplet, baseline and fusion experiments.
Background is estimated from an independent 64×64 blank-sky calibration frame matched to each exposure. Read variance is estimated as half the sample variance of the difference of two independent zero-light readout frames. These calibration noises use streams separate from search/template noise; 4096 calibration pixels support each estimate. Finite calibration-estimate uncertainty is omitted from the marginal variance diagnostic. Exact generator background/read-noise values do not enter the measurement pipeline.
title: Model Alerts

section: Truth labels detections; it never selects the easy ones
text:
Truth labels detections; it never selects the easy ones
After detection, we associate peaks to injected changes within the frozen radius. Unmatched detections remain negative examples. Bad pixels, cosmic rays, registration errors and local PSF mismatch all contribute candidates. A real change overlapping a detector artifact, or several associated real changes, is flagged as ambiguous.
Negative-family attribution uses the nearest associated cause; a genuine change takes label priority. Overlapping causes are counted separately from ambiguous associations. A brightening of a static star can overlap that star without making its binary label ambiguous. The persistent hot pixel contributes Poisson electrons in both the shared reference and every search exposure.


Science Explanation

Position association is an evaluation convention with finite coverage. A chance noise maximum near an injection can be associated; a badly displaced real peak can fall outside the radius. Report injection recovery, ambiguous counts and excluded challenge counts alongside classification metrics. A positive detected near a static star may include overlapping static residual light; the overlap flag makes that limitation visible. Do not use truth coordinates, family, filenames, field identity or split assignment as model features.
title: Model Alerts

text:
Build a native xScan dataset
The canonical arrays are search, template, difference, binary labels and split assignments, with candidate metadata stored separately. Raw cutouts remain in electron units for inspection. Model inputs use shared search/reference centering and scaling fitted only on eligible training rows; difference scaling is also fitted only on training rows.


Science Explanation

A normalization estimate is itself a learned quantity. Fitting it on all rows would expose held-out data even without their labels. Exact-stamp hashes are calculated in the units actually passed to the native fusion workflow.

section: Learn from images, from random weights
text:
Learn from images, from random weights
We compare native xScan pair and triplet transformer models initialized from scratch. The pair sees search and reference; the triplet also sees the xPois residual. Three initialization seeds are shown separately for each principal model. The same fields, candidates and optimization settings support a paired comparison.
All reference models and the permutation control complete the declared 12-epoch budget. We retain the checkpoint with lowest validation loss. The same validation fields select checkpoints and operating thresholds; their intervals are conditional development diagnostics and the precision expansion rule is a heuristic. Independent reserved fields supply the final endpoints.


Science Explanation

Training minimizes binary cross entropy from logits ziz_i,

ℒ=−1n∑i[yilog⁡σ(zi)+(1−yi)log⁡(1−σ(zi))].\mathcal L=-\frac1n\sum_i[y_i\log\sigma(z_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-\sigma(z_i))].

The sigmoid converts a logit to a score between zero and one. It does not make that score a calibrated astrophysical probability. Checkpoints are selected using validation loss. Our teaching configuration uses three encoder stages with embedding dimensions 16, 32 and 64, one block per stage, 12 epochs and Adam-style native optimizer settings. These are example choices, not a reproduction of a paper’s published accuracy. Quick smoke uses one epoch and fewer fields and cannot substantiate performance.

section: Can a simple measured statistic explain the result?
text:
Can a simple measured statistic explain the result?
SNR-only logistic regression is the first baseline. A second baseline adds positive core concentration, negative residual fraction, peak-to-RMS ratio and search/reference correlation. Nonfinite and repeated-extreme fractions are measured from raw pixels. Feature standardization and logistic coefficients are fitted on training rows only.
We measure nonfinite-pixel fraction and repeated-extreme fraction in every raw triplet and report their training ranges separately by class. Repeated extrema can expose clipping or quantization but do not establish its cause. No missing or clipped pixels are intentionally inserted.


Science Explanation

A high score can reflect a trivial generator cue rather than source morphology. The baselines expose how much signal comes from brightness or simple shape statistics. No family or injection-SNR column enters them. The expected injection SNR is log-uniform from four to 35 under an approximate background-dominated Gaussian calculation; measured detection SNR differs because of source noise, fitted subtraction and selection. Performance is conditional on this brightness and artifact mixture.

section: Ask the experiment to fail in a known way
text:
Ask the experiment to fail in a known way
We permute training labels once with a recorded seed and leave validation truth untouched. We also deliberately split candidates from one field across training and validation: the native provenance guard must reject that dataset before training. A development-only learning curve uses nested field subsets with their own training-only normalization.


Science Explanation

The permutation control tests whether genuine validation structure can be predicted from randomly assigned training targets. Unexpected predictability requires diagnosis, not a search for a more reassuring permutation seed. The invalid split is a guard demonstration and is never used to claim a performance gain. Learning curves help identify data limitation but cannot choose settings after final-test unblinding. Three initialization seeds show optimization sensitivity; they are not three independent sky surveys.

section: Does a measured xFit description add information?
text:
Does a measured xFit description add information?
The fusion investigation exports exact candidate difference stamps and row-aligned variance, fits the Gaussian difference model with xFit, then builds the native portable feature bundle. Candidate IDs and stamp hashes must correspond exactly. Native gates retain failed or invalid fits.


Science Explanation

An ideal single positive source has no negative lobe, while registration residuals can resemble positive/negative dipoles. Fitted shape, separation, fit quality and uncertainty can therefore add measured evidence. The Gaussian fit is an approximation to pixel-integrated sources and imperfect subtraction. A failed fit is an outcome with coverage implications, not a reason to discard a difficult candidate. Report fit_present, fit_valid and uncertainty coverage, along with fused classification metrics. Weights are marginal-variance approximations and omit residual covariance.

Native xFit feature transforms use fixed documented constants and row-local measurements, not a population-fitted scaler. The coverage receipt records those constants. Only image normalization uses training-estimated quantities.

section: Choose a validation operating point with tied scores
text:
Choose a validation operating point with tied scores
For every model and seed, we choose the highest threshold whose inclusive score >= threshold rule retains at least 95% of validation positives. Checkpoints, normalization and thresholds are frozen before generating or inferring the final reserved test set. The primary endpoint is test false-positive rate at that frozen threshold.


Science Explanation

Sort the n+n_+ positive validation scores in descending order. With k=⌈0.95n+⌉k=\lceil0.95n_+\rceil, choose t=s(k)t=s_{(k)}. Including every tie at tt may retain more than 95%; raising it would lose required positive examples.

TPR⁡(t)=TPTP+FN,FPR⁡(t)=FPFP+TN.\operatorname{TPR}(t)=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},\qquad
\operatorname{FPR}(t)=\frac{FP}{FP+TN}.

The native training workflow’s accuracy-selected threshold is not this operating point. Test recall is an achieved result, not automatically 95%. Invalidating bugs require a new freeze and fresh reserved seeds; earlier attempts remain recorded. Exploratory browser sliders do not alter the frozen endpoint reported in the scientific tables.

section: Separate detection recovery from classification retention
text:
Separate detection recovery from classification retention
Some injected changes never pass detection. A classifier cannot recover those missing candidates. We report detected associated injections divided by all injected ordinary changes, and final retained associated injections divided by that same injection denominator. Candidate-level recall has a different denominator: eligible detected positives.
The receipt decomposes detected injections into those with an eligible binary candidate and those detected only in excluded ambiguous/challenge associations. Classifier-rejected eligible injections are a separate loss. Each injection is counted once even if it matches several detections. Thus detection-to-retention loss is not attributed entirely to the classifier.


Science Explanation

An injection can create a complicated residual and a detection can overlap multiple causes. Injection recovery is counted by injection identity; classification confusion counts are counted by candidate identity. Neither quantity may silently replace the other. The detection threshold and association convention are part of the complete experiment, not fixed facts of the sky. Coverage tables identify movers, ambiguous associations and binary-eligible candidates for every split.

Association recovery does not prove that the change caused detection: a brightening can share a host registration residual. We report injected, detected and retained counts separately for appearances and brightenings. Appearances avoid this host-source residual confounding.
title: Model Alerts

section: Read curves and reliability at the modeled prevalence
text:
Read curves and reliability at the modeled prevalence
ROC tracks achieved recall against false-positive rate as score thresholds change. Precision–recall makes the class mixture more visible. Reliability compares score averages with observed positive fractions in occupied bins; Brier score averages squared score errors. We show each initialization seed rather than hiding outcomes behind a mean.


Science Explanation

Brier score is

BS=1N∑i(si−yi)2.\mathrm{BS}=\frac1N\sum_i(s_i-y_i)^2.

Empty reliability bins contain no evidence and remain empty. A small Brier score or a visually good reliability curve on this generator does not calibrate scores for an observed survey. ROC/PR curves and reliability use all eligible evaluation candidates, not the curated image gallery. The reported operating point remains the validation-frozen threshold.

predictions = {name: evaluation[key] for name, key in reference["score_arrays"].items()}
show(performance_diagnostics(evaluation["labels"], predictions))

text:
Uncertainty follows independent fields
We bootstrap fields, carrying every candidate and epoch in each sampled field together. Pair and triplet differences use the same resampled fields. The three initialization outcomes remain separate. Intervals are conditional on trained checkpoints, frozen thresholds and the specified modeled mixture.
Both reserved test and specified-shift populations receive field-bootstrap recall/FPR intervals. The validation sample is reused for checkpoint and threshold selection; its interval does not account for that selection.


Science Explanation

Independent-candidate bootstrap would overstate the information in repeated observations sharing a template. Field bootstrap samples field identities with replacement; repeated draws multiply all their candidates. Replicates without negatives have undefined FPR and are explicitly counted. The validation half-width rule is a development precision check, not a post-selection confidence guarantee. These percentile intervals do not include all training-population, generator-model or threshold-selection uncertainty.

title: Model Alerts

section: Explore the complete queue, inspect a bounded gallery
text:
Explore the complete queue, inspect a bounded gallery
Search, reference and signed difference panels share pan, zoom and tapped pixel selection. Exact raw pixel readouts remain in electron units even when display units change. Navigate candidates or filter by family and confusion outcome. The gallery contains at most 96 candidates selected by a recorded round-robin confusion/SNR/family rule. Empty categories remain empty.


Science Explanation

A human chooses a review budget as well as a desired completeness. At assumed positive prevalence π\pi, holding class-conditional score mixtures fixed,

purity=πTPRπTPR+(1−π)FPR,Nqueue=N[πTPR+(1−π)FPR].\mathrm{purity}=\frac{\pi\,TPR}{\pi\,TPR+(1-\pi)\,FPR},\qquad
N_{\mathrm{queue}}=N[\pi\,TPR+(1-\pi)\,FPR].

The browser recomputes these quantities from complete saved evaluation scores. It does not retrain or rerun inference. A prevalence change is not an arbitrary distribution shift: the projection assumes the positive and negative subpopulations keep their score distributions. Gallery counts are never substituted for population counts. Display transforms and page themes must leave raw data and equivalent scientific color scales unchanged.


gallery = np.load(root / "gallery.npz", allow_pickle=False)
rows = json.loads((root / "gallery-rows.json").read_text())
# The reference stores explicit original gallery indices and the full score pool.
explorer, gallery_rule = candidate_explorer(
    gallery["images"], rows, gallery["labels"], gallery["scores"],
    reference["inspector_threshold"], preselected=True,
    evaluation=dict(labels=evaluation["labels"],
                    scores=evaluation[reference["inspector_score_key"]],
                    snr=evaluation["snr"],
                    candidate_id=evaluation["candidate_id"],
                    family=evaluation["family"]))
show(explorer)
print(json.dumps(reference["gallery_rule"], indent=2))
